english_lines: Holding within it the life-breath,
‘one woman for one man,’
‘Domestic life is what is called virtue; even that,
is good if it brings no blame from another’ — says the,
Thirukkural; do not forget it,
do not stray from your direction,
The boat called life,
the lesson it gives,
within the human heart,
is a Veda impossible to forget,
(Life)
Youth is a costume that fades — in it,
the one who says ‘let whatever comes, come’ is a complete fool,
the one who guards before it comes is the wise one — before the storm,
the one who guards before it comes is the wise one,
the one who suffers after it comes is the dupe,
(Life)
A boat without oars — the waves,
will take it in every direction they call — a life with no one,
to block evil — that life too,
will become like the state of that boat.
notes: The opening `ஒருவனுக்கு ஒருத்தி` is retained directly as `one woman for one man`; it is not paraphrased into a modern abstract term such as monogamy.
The Thirukkural wording is translated exactly from the verified anthology witness. No canonical-edition wording is substituted for what this page prints.
`வாழ்க்கை எனும் ஓடம்` remains the boat-called-life metaphor and `மறக்க வொண்ணா வேதம்` remains an unforgettable Veda rather than generic wisdom.
Youth remains a fading costume, and the repeated warning to guard before the storm remains repeated.
The final boat-without-oars analogy retains waves actively calling directions and a life lacking someone who blocks evil.

translator_notes: The translation retains the song's moral-didactic architecture: one-woman/one-man life-breath, the anthology's printed Thirukkural wording, life-as-boat, Veda, youth-as-fading-costume, storm-preparedness and the oarless-boat warning.
No alternate Thirukkural edition or soundtrack wording is used to repair or harmonize the source.
